services.title: Boiler repairs
services.text: No heating, no hot water, odd noises or a fault code on the display. We find the cause and explain it plainly.

services.title: Central heating

services.text: Programmers, room thermostats and smart controls, fitted and set up so you understand them.

emergency.intro: Some problems cannot wait. These are the first things to do while help is on the way. They are general guidance for a demonstration, not professional advice.

cards.title: If you smell gas
steps: Do not use light switches, sockets, doorbells or anything that could spark.
Do not smoke or use a naked flame.
Open doors and windows.
Turn off the gas at the meter if you can do it safely.
Leave the property and call the national gas emergency number from outside. It is printed on your gas bill and near your meter.
Any repair afterwards must be done by a Gas Safe registered engineer.

cards.title: If your carbon monoxide alarm sounds
steps: Open doors and windows and get everyone outside into fresh air.
Turn off gas appliances if you can do it safely on the way out.
If anyone feels unwell (headache, dizziness, sickness), get medical help straight away.
Call the national gas emergency number from outside.
Do not use the appliance again until a Gas Safe registered engineer has checked it.

cards.title: If a pipe bursts or water is pouring
steps: Turn off the water at the stopcock (usually under the kitchen sink).
If water is near electrics, sockets or a light fitting, do not touch them. Turn the electricity off at the consumer unit only if you can reach it while standing somewhere dry.
Open the cold taps to drain the pipes.
Catch what you can with buckets and towels.
Ring us, or any plumber, and tell them the water is off.

cards.title: If the heating fails in a cold snap
steps: Check the boiler display for a fault code and write it down.
Look at the pressure gauge and compare it with the normal range in your boiler manual.
In freezing weather, check the condensate pipe outside (see the guide below).
Keep one room warm with a safe portable heater and keep doors closed.
Ring us and tell us if anyone in the house is vulnerable to the cold.

disclaimer: General guidance, sample text for a demonstration, not professional advice.
gasLine: Anything involving gas: call a Gas Safe registered engineer. Never open up a boiler or gas appliance yourself.

guides.title: Bleeding a radiator
guides.summary: A radiator that is cold at the top usually has air trapped in it. Letting the air out is a common household job.
need: A radiator key (from a hardware shop)
steps: Turn the heating off and wait until the radiators are cool to the touch.
Find the bleed valve: a small square fitting at one top corner of the radiator.
Hold the cloth under the valve and fit the key.
Turn the key slowly anticlockwise, about a quarter turn. You should hear a hiss as air escapes.
When water starts to dribble out instead of air, turn the key back clockwise to close it. Do not overtighten.
Check the boiler pressure gauge afterwards. Bleeding can lower it (see the boiler pressure guide).
Turn the heating back on and check the radiator warms evenly.
guides.stop: If the valve will not turn, is damaged, or water keeps coming after you close it, stop and call a heating engineer.

guides.title: Topping up boiler pressure
guides.summary: Many combi boilers lose a little pressure over time. Your manual explains how to top it up using the filling loop.
need: Your boiler manual (most are online under the model name)
steps: Find the pressure gauge on the boiler or just below it. Most gauges have a marked normal range.
Read the manual for your exact boiler before you touch anything. Filling loops differ between makes.
With the heating off and the system cool, locate the filling loop: usually a flexible hose or a built-in key or lever under the boiler.
Open the valves slowly, as the manual describes, and watch the gauge rise.
Close the valves once the needle is within the normal range shown in your manual. Do not go above it.
If your filling loop is a detachable hose, follow your manual about whether to remove it afterwards.
guides.stop: If the pressure keeps dropping, if you see water leaking, or if you are unsure which part is which, stop and call a Gas Safe registered engineer. Never remove the boiler casing.

guides.title: Thawing a frozen condensate pipe
guides.summary: Condensing boilers drain water through a plastic pipe, often running outside. In a hard frost it can freeze and stop the boiler.
need: A kettle or jug of warm water
steps: Check the display. Some boilers show a specific fault code or a gurgling noise when the condensate pipe is blocked.
Follow the grey or white plastic pipe from the boiler to where it leaves the house and runs to a drain.
Look for the frozen part, often the lowest bend or the open end.
Pour warm water (not boiling) slowly along the pipe, or hold a warm cloth on it.
Take care not to create ice on the ground where you or others walk.
Once it is clear, reset the boiler following your manual.
guides.stop: Never use boiling water or a flame. If you cannot reach the pipe safely, or the boiler will not restart, call a Gas Safe registered engineer.

guides.title: Finding your stopcock
guides.summary: The stopcock turns off the water to the whole house. Knowing where it is before you need it saves a lot of mess.
steps: Look under the kitchen sink first. This is the most common place.
If it is not there, check a downstairs toilet, airing cupboard, utility room, cellar or under the stairs.
It looks like a tap or lever on a pipe, often where the water supply comes in through the floor.
Turn it clockwise to close. It may be stiff if it has not been used for years.
Turn it back anticlockwise to open, then back a fraction so it does not stick.
Label it and tell everyone in the house where it is.
guides.stop: If it will not move with hand pressure, do not force it with tools. Ring a plumber to free or replace it.

guides.title: A dripping tap
guides.summary: Most drips come from a worn washer or cartridge. Whether you change it yourself depends on the type of tap.
need: Replacement washer or cartridge to match
steps: Put the plug in so small parts cannot fall down the drain.
Turn off the water to the tap, using the isolation valve under the sink or the stopcock.
Open the tap to let the remaining water out.
Remove the handle cover and loosen the headgear, as the tap maker describes.
Swap the washer or cartridge for a matching one.
Reassemble, turn the water back on slowly and check for drips.
guides.stop: If the tap body is cracked, the fittings are seized, or you cannot isolate the water, leave it and book a plumber.

guides.title: A toilet that keeps running
guides.summary: Water trickling into the pan after a flush usually means the fill valve or the flush valve seal needs attention.
steps: Lift the cistern lid carefully and put it somewhere safe. It is heavy and breaks easily.
Watch the water level. If it rises above the overflow, the fill valve needs adjusting.
Most fill valves have an adjuster or a float you can lower a little.
If water runs into the pan without reaching the overflow, the flush valve seal is probably worn.
Isolate the water and follow the maker's instructions to replace the seal, or book a plumber.
guides.stop: If you see cracks in the cistern or water around the base of the toilet, turn the water off and call a plumber.

guides.title: A slow or blocked sink
guides.summary: Grease, hair and food build up in the trap under the sink. Clearing it by hand is often enough.
steps: Remove the plug and any visible debris from the plughole.
Block the overflow with a damp cloth and use the plunger with a little water in the sink.
If that does not work, put a bucket under the trap (the U-shaped pipe) and unscrew it by hand.
Clean it out, check the seals and screw it back hand tight.
Run water and check for leaks under the sink.
guides.stop: Avoid mixing drain chemicals. If several drains are slow at once, the problem is further down and needs a plumber or drainage company.

guides.title: Radiator cold at the bottom
guides.summary: A radiator that is warm at the top and cold at the bottom often has sludge settled inside it.
need: A note of which radiators are affected
steps: With the heating on, feel the radiator from top to bottom, taking care as it may be hot.
Note which radiators are cold at the bottom and which are fine.
If it is only one radiator, it may need removing and flushing.
If several are affected, the whole system may need cleaning.
Tell your engineer what you found when you book.
guides.stop: Flushing a system and removing radiators is work for a heating engineer.

guides.title: One radiator will not warm up
guides.summary: A single cold radiator is often down to a closed valve or a stuck thermostatic valve pin.
steps: Check both valves at the ends of the radiator are open.
If it has a thermostatic head with numbers, turn it to its highest setting.
Remove the head (most unscrew by hand) and look for a small pin underneath.
Press the pin gently. It should spring back. If it is stuck down, it can sometimes be freed by tapping it lightly.
Refit the head and give the radiator time to warm.
guides.stop: If the pin will not move or water appears around the valve, stop and call a heating engineer.

guides.title: Understanding your thermostat and timer
guides.summary: The room thermostat decides when the house is warm enough. The timer decides when heating is allowed to run.
need: The manual for your controls, or the model name
steps: Find the room thermostat. It is often in a hallway or living room.
Find the timer or programmer, usually near the boiler or in the airing cupboard.
Set the timer for the hours you are normally at home and awake.
Set the room thermostat to a comfortable setting and leave it, rather than turning it up and down.
Use the radiator valves to make individual rooms cooler.
Check the clock on the timer after a power cut or clock change.
guides.stop: If the controls do not seem to switch the boiler on and off, ask a heating engineer to check the wiring and settings.

guides.title: Getting ready for a boiler service
guides.summary: A few minutes before the engineer arrives makes the visit quicker.
need: Your previous service record if you have it
steps: Clear a path to the boiler and space around it.
Have the make and model to hand.
Note any noises, leaks or fault codes you have seen since the last service.
Know where your gas meter and stopcock are.
Ask to see the engineer's Gas Safe ID card when they arrive.
guides.stop: If anyone offers to service a gas boiler without being Gas Safe registered, do not let them.

guides.title: Going away in winter
guides.summary: An empty, unheated house is where frozen and burst pipes tend to happen.
steps: Leave the heating on a frost or low setting rather than off. Your controls manual explains the frost setting.
Open loft hatches and under-sink cupboards so warm air reaches the pipes.
Check outside taps are isolated and drained if they have their own valve.
Leave a key and the stopcock location with a neighbour.
Ask someone to look in if the weather turns very cold.
guides.stop: If you come back to a leak or no water, turn off the stopcock and call a plumber.

guides.title: Lagging exposed pipes
guides.summary: Foam lagging on pipes in lofts, garages and outside walls helps stop them freezing.
need: Foam pipe lagging to fit your pipe size
steps: Find pipes in unheated places: loft, garage, outside walls, under floors.
Measure the pipe width and buy lagging to fit.
Slip the lagging over the pipe and tape the joins.
Cover bends and valves as well as straight runs.
Leave stopcocks and valves easy to reach.
guides.stop: Take care in lofts: step only on joists or boards, and do not lift insulation near electrical fittings.

guides.title: Low water pressure at a tap
guides.summary: If only one tap is weak, the problem is often a clogged filter or a part-closed valve.
steps: Check whether the problem is one tap, one room or the whole house.
For a single tap, unscrew the aerator on the end of the spout and clean it.
Check the isolation valve under the sink is fully open.
If the whole house is affected, ask neighbours. It may be a supply issue for your water company.
Check the stopcock is fully open.
guides.stop: If pressure drops suddenly with no reason, or you can hear water running when all taps are off, there may be a leak. Call a plumber.

guides.title: Banging or noisy pipes
guides.summary: Knocking, banging and whistling pipes usually point to loose clips, air, or water pressure changes.
need: A note of when the noise happens
steps: Note when it happens: when a tap closes, when the heating starts, or all the time.
Banging when a tap shuts quickly can be water hammer. Try closing taps more slowly.
Look for pipes you can see that move when water runs. Loose clips can often be tightened.
Gurgling in radiators can mean air. See the radiator bleeding guide.
Kettling noises from a boiler need an engineer to look at it.
guides.stop: Any loud or new noise from the boiler itself: stop using it if it sounds wrong and call a Gas Safe registered engineer.

guides.title: Carbon monoxide alarms
guides.summary: Carbon monoxide has no smell or colour. An audible alarm is the way to know it is there.
steps: Fit an alarm in any room with a fuel-burning appliance, following the maker's instructions.
Test it regularly with the test button.
Know the difference between the alarm sound and the low battery chirp.
Replace it at the end of its life. The date is on the back.
Learn the warning signs: headaches, dizziness, sickness that ease when you go outside.
guides.stop: If it sounds, follow the emergency steps on this page and get a Gas Safe registered engineer to check appliances.

guides.title: If you smell gas
guides.time: Read now, before you need it
guides.summary: What to do in the first minutes if you smell gas at home.
need: Know where your gas meter is
Know where the emergency number is printed (gas bill and near the meter)
steps: Do not touch light switches, sockets or anything that could spark.
Put out any naked flames and do not smoke.
Open doors and windows.
Turn off the gas at the meter if you can safely reach it.
Leave the property and call the national gas emergency number from outside.
Wait for help outside.
guides.stop: Never try to find or fix a gas leak yourself. All gas work must be done by a Gas Safe registered engineer.

guides.title: Shower running cold or weak
guides.summary: A cold or weak shower can be a blocked head, a hot water problem or a faulty valve.
steps: Check other hot taps. If they are cold too, the problem is the hot water supply, not the shower.
Unscrew the shower head and soak it to remove limescale.
Check the hose is not kinked.
For an electric shower, check its own switch and trip at the consumer unit.
Run it again and note what changed.
guides.stop: Electric showers and their wiring are for a qualified electrician. Gas hot water problems need a Gas Safe registered engineer.

guides.title: A leak under the sink
guides.summary: A slow drip in the cupboard under the sink is easy to miss and worth catching early.
steps: Empty the cupboard and dry everything with kitchen roll.
Run the tap and watch with a torch to see where the water appears.
If it is the waste trap, hand tighten the joints and check the seals.
If it is a supply pipe or valve, turn off the isolation valve or stopcock.
Put a bowl underneath and book a plumber.
guides.stop: If the cupboard floor is soft or swollen, the leak may have been there a while. Turn the water off and call a plumber.

faq.q: Do you charge a call-out fee?
faq.a: We tell you the price of the visit on the phone before we book it, so there are no surprises. (In this demonstration there are no real prices.)
Not on this site. We book by phone so we can ask the right questions. This site is static and has no booking system.

faq.q: Are your engineers Gas Safe registered?
faq.a: A real heating firm must be for any gas work, and you should always ask to see the ID card. This is a fictional demonstration, so there are no engineers here.

faq.q: Are the guides on this site professional advice?
faq.a: No. They are general guidance, written as sample text for a demonstration. If in doubt, stop and call a qualified engineer.
